messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out: Going out, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Therapy Content: avoid thinking about anything discussed in therapy
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 68-year-old widowed dancer who came to therapy reluctantly, referred by his primary care physician after his blood pressure spiked during a routine checkup and he admitted he had not left his apartment in three weeks. The trouble began eighteen months ago, when he was driving home from a rehearsal through a late-winter rainstorm. A delivery truck ran a red light and T-boned his sedan on the driver’s side. Kwame remembers the impact—the way the world went sideways, the shriek of metal—but after that, the memory fractures. He has only fragments: the smell of gasoline, a stranger’s hand on his shoulder, the paramedic asking his name. He cannot tell a clear story of what happened, even to himself. When he tries to deliberately recall the sequence, his mind goes blank, and he is left with only a pulsing dread and the certainty that something terrible occurred that he cannot fully grasp.

That incomplete picture has become a source of deep shame. Kwame has built his life on control and precision—forty years as a professional dancer, then another decade teaching—and now he cannot even trust his own memory. He has come to believe that if he cannot hold the event in his mind, he cannot be sure he did not somehow cause it. This self-doubt has spread into a broader conviction that his body, once his most reliable instrument, can no longer be trusted. He feels it might fail him at any moment—his knees buckle when he stands too fast, his hands tremble when he reaches for a cup, and he is certain that if he tried to dance now, his legs would give way. The feeling of institutional failure compounds this: the other driver was never charged, the insurance company dragged the claim out for months, and Kwame is left with the bitter sense that the systems meant to protect him had simply let him fall through the cracks.

Because he cannot trust his own body or his own mind, Kwame has narrowed his world. He stopped going out entirely after the third month, convinced that any trip outside—even to the corner store—would expose him to another catastrophe. He avoids seeing the people he used to socialize with before the event; their faces remind him of the person he was, and he fears they will see how diminished he has become. When his therapist gently suggested they explore the accident in more detail, Kwame found himself canceling the next two sessions, avoiding thinking about anything discussed in therapy because the very act of remembering felt like opening a door he could not close.

The threat is everywhere now. At home, Kwame feels unsafe unless his back is against a wall where he can see the entire room; he has rearranged his furniture so that his armchair sits in a corner, facing the door. When something takes longer than expected—a delivery, a repairman, even a pot of water coming to a boil—he assumes something bad is happening, that someone is hurt or that disaster is unfolding just out of sight. Unexpected or loud sounds send him into a state of high alert: a car horn outside, a dropped pan in the kitchen, the bang of a neighbor’s door—each one makes his heart slam and his breath catch, and he stands rigid until he can confirm no one is coming for him. The more he stays inside, the more his vigilance sharpens; every creak of the building, every footstep in the hallway feels like a signal of danger. He has come to believe that the only way to stay safe is to stay still and keep watch, and that belief has locked him into a cycle he cannot break on his own.

What finally brought Kwame to seek help was not the isolation or the fear, but a single moment three weeks ago. He was standing in his kitchen, back to the counter, when he heard a truck backfire two blocks away. He dropped to the floor, covering his head, and stayed there for forty minutes, unable to move. When he finally got up, he looked at his reflection in the dark window and did not recognize the man staring back. He is afraid—afraid that therapy will force him to remember what he cannot bear to hold, afraid that his body will never feel like his own again—but he is also afraid of spending whatever years he has left pressed against a wall, waiting for the next sound.
